A proposal from the Trump administration to revise the Endangered Species Act could have critical impacts on vulnerable animals, plants and habitats across the U.S., environmental advocates say.

Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of the Interior outlined several ESA rules it plans to roll back, including changes to the listing of protected species and critical habitat under 50 CFR part 424. According to the Interior Department, those decisions would be based on the "best scientific and commercial data available."

Advocates argue the changes could allow economics to influence what had previously been science-based decision-making. Susan Holmes, executive director of the Endangered Species Coalition, said that could put financial interests ahead of protections for species such as the Florida panther.

Conservation groups including Humane World for Animals and Defenders of Wildlife warned that this would weaken safeguards by depriving newly listed species of automatic protection from killing, trapping and other prohibited "take." Species proposed for listing, including the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse and Monarch butterfly, could be affected.

The administration is also seeking to narrow the definition of critical habitat under 50 CFR part 17 to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Holmes said habitat loss remains the leading driver of extinction and that protecting where species live, breed and feed is essential to recovery.

Changes to interagency cooperation rules under 50 CFR part 402 would, critics say, make it easier for agencies to approve projects such as mining, drilling and logging without fully assessing impacts on species and habitat. The Interior Department said the proposal would restore the 2019 consultation framework.

Since the ESA was passed in 1973, a 2019 study found it has saved 99% of listed species from extinction. A 30-day public comment period is now underway following the proposal.

EAST PALESTINE, Ohio — Two years after a Norfolk Southern train derailment spewed a toxic cloud that drove thousands from their homes, freight trains carrying the same chemicals central to that disaster continue to roll through town, with few major steps taken by lawmakers to prevent another accident.

A Howard Center for Investigative Journalism analysis of private train movement data found that, at least twice a week on average, a Norfolk Southern train with cars displaying hazardous material placards for vinyl chloride and butyl acrylate passes through East Palestine. Norfolk Southern trains with at least one car marked as carrying hazardous materials pass the derailment site about 10 times a day on average.

That information is not readily available to residents or most elected officials. Railroads are not required to disclose such detailed cargo information to local governments in advance, leaving communities with little way of knowing exactly what moves through town.

On Feb. 3, 2023, an equipment failure caused 38 cars of a Norfolk Southern freight train — including 11 carrying hazardous materials — to derail. Local volunteer firefighters responded quickly, but did not initially have access to AskRail, the industry app used by authorized first responders to identify cargo.
